agenten-gedaechtnis.summary: Claude Code, Hermes, and other clients store their session notes in a dedicated workspace and get them back for the matching directory next time. This is deliberately separated from curated knowledge: raw transcripts may be cleaned up and discarded.

details.p1: At the end of a session, the client deposits a condensed note; on the next run, it gets back the notes matching the working directory. That way, a fresh session knows what was decided last week without you repeating it. With the hooks of the Claude Code plugin, this happens automatically.
details.p2: The memory is a dedicated workspace designated as such in its settings. The separation is key: curated knowledge is written by a human because it is worth it, while transcripts are created automatically and may be cleaned up or discarded at any time. Automatic transcripts therefore never belong in the curated area.
details.p3: What is saved is a condensation, never the raw conversation. Notes are ordinary pages—readable, searchable, editable, and deletable like everything else—and what an agent is allowed to do is determined by its workspace membership, not its token.

agenten-gedaechtnis.where: A workspace is designated as memory in its settings.

von-mir-geteilt.title: Everything I have shared, in one place
von-mir-geteilt.summary: A list of all shares you granted yourself, across all workspaces. If you know you shared something, but no longer which page it was, you will find it here and can revoke it with a click and a confirmation.

details.p1: In the account menu at top right, “Shares” leads to a page with two tabs. “Shared by me” is the first: each row lists the page, the workspace it belongs to, who it went to or whether it is a public link, whether viewing or editing is allowed, how far it reaches, and until when. Once there are six or more shares, a filter field for page title, workspace, and address appears above.
details.p2: Initially, only shares currently active are shown. Revoked and expired ones are brought up by the “Show ended” toggle, because “that was open until March” is part of the answer. “Revoke” asks for confirmation first and explains the effect: a public link is gone forever, while a share to an account can be granted again in the page’s share dialog.
details.p3: The list shows only what you shared yourself, and only from workspaces where you are still a member. What others shared in a workspace is found in its overview under “Open shares”. Only admins in the respective workspace can revoke; if you no longer hold that role there, the row remains and explains that, instead of showing a button that would fail.

von-mir-geteilt.where: Account menu at top right, “Shares”, “Shared by me” tab.

seiten-teilen.title: Share a page externally
seiten-teilen.summary: A page can be shared individually: as a link that anyone who has it can open, or with a specific account to view or edit. Optionally just the page or everything beneath it, optionally with an expiration, revokable at any time.

details.p1: In the page menu, you find “Share…”. There you first decide on the scope: just this page, or including everything nested beneath it. Then you have two paths. “To an account” gives the page to someone who already has an account here to view or edit; the person does not need to become a member of any workspace and sees nothing else from it. “Create link” produces an address where the page can be read without logging in. The address is then listed with a copy button in the dialog and under “Shares” in the account menu for as long as the link is valid. Anyone who is an admin in the workspace can view it; everyone else sees only its first characters. For links created before 2026-09-24, the address is not stored: there, the row offers to generate a new link with the same scope.
details.p2: A link is always read-only. Writing via an address that someone can pass around does not exist here—not as a setting, but not at all. A share to an account can write, because behind it stands a signed-in person who appears in the page history like anyone else.
details.p3: Revocation takes effect immediately, even for someone who has the page open right now: the connection is re-checked and dropped. It will not take back what has already been read, which is why eXocortex asks once more when creating a link. A share “with everything below” is tied to the structure, not a list: a page you move within the shared area stays shared, and one you move out is no longer shared.
details.p4: The reverse case is the dangerous one, which is why eXocortex announces it: moving a page into an already shared area shares it along. When filing it, a warning appears before the move takes place, and a page that is shared from higher up bears the “Shared” badge at the top, even if nothing was configured on the page itself.
details.p5: Whoever receives a page learns about it by email: when it is shared, when what is permitted, how far it extends, or how long it is valid changes later on, and when you revoke the share. The email states who shared it, which page it is about, and what is allowed with it, along with a link directly there. The revocation email only mentions the title and leads to the list of what remains shared, since the page itself is now closed. No email is sent for a link (it belongs to no one) or when moving a page into a shared area, otherwise tidying up would result in a hundred emails.

freigaben-uebersicht.title: What is shared, and what has been given to me
freigaben-uebersicht.summary: Two lists: all shares of a workspace in one place, for tidying up, and the pages that others have shared with you. The latter appear in no navigation, because you are not a member of that workspace.

details.p1: In workspace settings, “Open shares” leads to the list of what has been granted outward from here: which page, to whom or as a link, read-only or writing, how far, until when. Revoked shares remain listed instead of disappearing, because “that was open until March” is part of the answer. Without this list, “what of ours is actually public” is a question nobody can answer after a year.
details.p2: In the account menu top right, “Shares”, under the “Shared with me” tab, leads in the opposite direction: pages that someone has given you, across workspaces. They do not appear in any page tree, because you are not a member there; this list is the only way to them. Such a page opens without the navigation of the foreign workspace: you see the page and, if the area was included, what hangs below it, nothing else.
details.p3: What you reach via a share, you cannot pass on. A shared page has no “Share” button: who may pass it on is a question for the workspace it comes from.

freigaben-uebersicht.where: Account menu top right, “Shares”, “Shared with me” tab; workspace settings, “Open shares”.

projekt-archive.title: Importing and exporting a project as a ZIP
projekt-archive.summary: An entire project goes out as a ZIP and comes back in as a ZIP, for moving or as a handoff to someone without access. Existing files are only overwritten if you explicitly request it.

details.p1: Exporting packs the entire file tree into a ZIP, with folders and attachments. That is the way out: sending it to a publisher’s editorial team, moving to another system, or simply taking a copy in hand that works without eXocortex.
details.p2: Importing goes back in the same direction and accepts a ZIP from elsewhere, such as a university template. The files are brought in all at once, not individually, so an abort does not leave half a project behind.
details.p3: Existing files are left untouched unless you explicitly request overwriting. The bytes travel as a normal attachment, so there is no second transfer channel alongside the one that is already there for files anyway.

projekt-archive.where: The menu of the project view.

synctex.title: Jump from source code into the PDF and back
synctex.summary: A click in the source code jumps to the matching spot in the PDF, a click in the PDF back into the source code. In a long document, that is the difference between searching and finding.

details.p1: Double-clicking in the source code scrolls the PDF to the spot corresponding to that line and highlights it briefly. Double-clicking in the PDF opens the associated file at the right line, even if the paragraph comes from an included file you did not even remember existed.
details.p2: The mapping comes from the map recorded during the typesetting run. Both directions are also available as tools, so an agent can ask where a source code line ends up in the PDF or which line lies behind a spot in the PDF.
details.p3: The PDF is displayed in the built-in viewer based on pdf.js. Embedding a third-party viewer is forbidden by the security policy of this deployment, and for good reason: this way the PDF stays in the same page and not in a foreign frame.

synctex.where: Double-click in the editor or in the PDF of the project view.

projekt-bauen.title: Build with latexmk, including error list
projekt-bauen.summary: Building runs with latexmk in a container on the server, without needing anything installed locally. Errors and warnings come back as a list instead of a desert of logs, and a build can be cancelled.

details.p1: Clicking “Build” sends the project to latexmk in a container on the server. Nothing needs to be installed on your machine, not even the two gigabytes of TeX Live, and it works just the same on someone else’s machine.
details.p2: What comes back is the PDF and a list of errors and warnings with file and line, all clickable. That is the practical difference from a terminal: instead of searching two thousand lines of log output for the one missing brace, you click the error and land right at the spot.
details.p3: The full log is still available in case the list is not enough. A build can be cancelled, older builds remain accessible along with their results, and all of this is also available as a tool, allowing an agent to build, read the error, fix it, and build again.

projekt-bauen.where: The “Build” button in the project view.

render-vorlagen.title: Custom layouts for the PDF
render-vorlagen.summary: What the PDF looks like is defined in a template that can be created and edited: font, margins, headers, title page. This allows a letter to look different from a report, without anything on the page itself being different.

details.p1: A template provides the typesetting instructions for the PDF: font family and size, page margins, headers and footers, title page, numbering, hyphenation language. When publishing, you choose which one to use; nothing changes on the page itself.
details.p2: You create as many as you have kinds of documents. A letter with an address field, a report with a cover sheet and table of contents, a flyer with nothing at all: the same page, three results. Templates can be edited and deleted, and agents can manage them using tools.
details.p3: The fonts must be available in the typesetting container. That is why this deployment uses a custom image with the desired fonts; otherwise xelatex falls back to a substitute font, and the result looks different from what the template specifies.

pdf-veroeffentlichen.title: Having a page typeset as a PDF
pdf-veroeffentlichen.summary: A page passes through Pandoc and xelatex and returns as a typeset PDF attached to the page as an ordinary attachment. If the page changes, the PDF indicates that it is outdated; if nothing changes, invoking it again costs nothing.

details.p1: You trigger publishing via the page menu, typesetting runs in the background on the server, and you get a PDF that looks like a book rather than a screen printout: proper paragraph breaks, hyphenation, headers, table of contents, formulas typeset instead of rendered as an image.
details.p2: The finished PDF is attached to the page as an ordinary attachment. That means: downloadable, deletable, visible in the history, searchable just like any other file. An agent can read it too, which is how it checks whether its output truly looks the way it should.
details.p3: A checksum is computed from the content, serving two purposes at once: cache and outdated indicator. If you change nothing, calling it a second time costs nothing and returns the same file. If you change the page, the PDF shows that it no longer matches the text. A run can be tracked, cancelled, and examined via its log in case of errors.

pdf-veroeffentlichen.where: In the page menu under “Publish as PDF”.

projekte.title: LaTeX projects with a real file tree
projekte.summary: A project is a page whose content is not body text, but a file tree: .tex, .bib, images, subfolders. It is edited in the browser, collaboratively and in real time just like a normal page.

details.p1: For a thesis, a book, or an article with a bibliography, a single page is not enough: you need multiple .tex files, a .bib, figures, and subfolders. A project is exactly that, and it still sits in the tree like any other page, with the same permissions and the same search.
details.p2: The file tree is on the left, the source code with syntax highlighting on the right, and next to it the compiled PDF. Editing happens collaboratively and in real time, just like on a normal page, because the same mechanism powers it underneath. You can create, rename, move, and delete files, and upload images or other assets alongside them.
details.p3: Agents can edit the same tree, including targeted changes to specific spots in a file. An external change takes the same path as typing in the browser, so it appears immediately in the open editor and not just in the database.

projekte.where: Create a new page and choose create as project.

push-benachrichtigungen.title: Notifications on mobile and desktop
push-benachrichtigungen.summary: eXocortex can nudge you on your devices when you are not looking: shortly before an event, on a comment on your page, and when an agent deliberately notifies you. You configure per device which device hears what.

details.p1: Under Settings → Notifications, you register the device you are currently sitting at. The browser asks for permission once; after that, the device appears in the list. Each device has separate switches for the three types, because the phone in your pocket and the computer at work rarely want to hear the same things. A test message right next to it shows immediately whether it arrives.
details.p2: The three types are: shortly before an event from your calendar, a comment on a page you wrote or a reply in a thread you are already part of, and messages from agents. The last one is the real reason for the feature: a long run is finished, something went wrong, a question is blocking progress, and Hermes or a Claude Code session reaches you directly on your phone via exo_push_send instead of you having to check.
details.p3: The text of the notification is encrypted to your device: the push service in between, meaning Google, Mozilla, or Apple, carries an envelope it cannot open. Tapping it opens the page in question in an already open window instead of opening a second one.
details.p4: On iPhone and iPad, notifications are only available if eXocortex is installed via “Add to Home Screen”; this is a limitation of Safari. If you unregister a device or revoke permission in the browser, it stops immediately; a device the push service no longer recognizes is dropped from the list automatically.

benachrichtigungen-einstellen.title: Decide for yourself what you receive mail about
benachrichtigungen-einstellen.summary: Under Settings → Notifications, you can see in one place when eXocortex reaches out to you on its own: on your devices and by email. The email part applies to the whole account, the device part to each device individually.

details.p1: The page separates two questions that are easily conflated. A device decides for itself, because your phone in the evening should hear something different from the computer at work. Your address, on the other hand, belongs to you and not to a browser, which is why an email setting applies everywhere equally, no matter where you currently sign in.
details.p2: By email, there are three entries. The first is a toggle for shared pages. It covers all three cases someone informs you about via a share: that a page newly arrives with you, that your permissions on it change, and that access is revoked again. It is turned on by default, because a share you never learn about is of no use to you. If you turn it off, no email is queued at all, instead of sending one and discarding it.
details.p3: The second is comments, and that one has three options instead of two: never, immediately, or collected once a day. By default, it is set to “never”, because comments reach you on your devices anyway and no one should receive unsolicited mail. If you turn it on, you receive one email per page with the names and the first words, plus a link to the page. A full comment is never included in the email: the conversation happens on the page, not in your inbox.
details.p4: Even “immediately” buffers briefly, for about two minutes. If someone types four replies in a row in a thread, they should send you one email and not four. The daily digest does the same across a whole day and goes out in the morning; exactly when is configured by administration for the entire installation. If a share is removed in the meantime, the affected page drops out of the pending digest instead of showing you its title again.
details.p5: The third notifies you about automations that are no longer running: a rule that disabled itself after repeated errors, or the first failed run of a scheduled rule. It is enabled by default, because otherwise no one tells you that a rule has not done anything for days.
details.p6: Only options that this installation actually delivers are offered. A combination of trigger and channel for which there is no sender neither appears as a toggle nor can it be set via the tools: a switch that does nothing is worse than a missing one.
details.p7: Agents see and set the same preferences via exo_notification_preferences and exo_notification_preference_set. For push, exo_push_device_update remains responsible, because that refers to the individual device and not the account.

token-seitenbereiche.title: Restrict a token to specific pages
token-seitenbereiche.summary: An access token can be pinned to a page or a page range when created. After that, it cannot access anything else: not via search, not via links, not via lists, and the rest simply does not exist for this token.

details.p1: When creating a token, there is a “Restrict to pages” section under permissions. You select a workspace, then one or more pages, and for each page whether only it is meant or everything beneath it. Without specifying anything, the token remains as broad as your account, as it always was.
details.p2: This is intended for agents that should only know a specific section: a writing assistant for “Worldbuilding > Cyberpunk” does not need to see your tax documents and should not even know they exist. The boundary therefore applies not only to directly opening a page, but also to search, page tree, links, related pages, attachments, trash, and filing suggestions. A call referencing the entire workspace is rejected rather than filtered, ensuring nothing slips through that nobody thought of.
details.p3: A token can never have more permissions than the account behind it: upon creation, every listed page is verified as a read operation by you, and on every request, your current membership applies additionally. A restricted token also cannot create an unrestricted one. If the last page a token was restricted to is deleted, it can access nothing at all, instead of regaining access to everything.

token-seitenbereiche.where: Settings, Connections, when creating a token.

mcp-abonnements.title: An agent learns about a change instead of asking
mcp-abonnements.summary: A client can subscribe to a page and gets notified when it changes. Every notification is checked against permissions at the moment it is written, so revoked access receives no further updates.

details.p1: Without a subscription, the only option for an agent is to ask every few seconds whether something has changed. With a subscription, eXocortex notifies it on its own as soon as the page changes. This saves calls and enables collaboration where you write and an agent reacts to it.
details.p2: Every single notification is checked against permissions at the moment it is written, not at the moment the subscription was created. Revoked access therefore receives nothing more, even if the connection is still open; revoking access closes it.
details.p3: There is no screen for this; the client does it on its own. A subscription to a page that does not exist is accepted rather than rejected, because a rejection would give away whether that page exists.

mcp-abonnements.where: No screen: the client subscribes on its own.

verbindungen.title: Get rid of connected clients
verbindungen.summary: Every granted connection is listed and can be severed with one click. Severed access ends immediately, even for an active connection.

details.p1: The list shows every client you have granted access to, with name, timestamp, and permissions. That turns “who actually has access to my notes” into a page rather than a memory exercise.
details.p2: Severing takes effect immediately, not just at the next login. An active connection is dropped rather than curtailed after the fact, because an existing connection whose permissions are stripped away is harder to get right than one that has to be established anew.
details.p3: The same applies in reverse: expanded permissions only arrive with a fresh connection. In addition, open connections are regularly checked to ensure they are still authorized, in case a message is lost.

mcp-ueber-http.title: Connect clients that only know an address
mcp-ueber-http.summary: Alongside the local process, MCP over HTTP is available with its own login server, for clients like ChatGPT that cannot hold a token. Before a connection is established, you must confirm it on an approval page.

details.p1: Some clients run on your computer and can start a local process; others run in the cloud and only know an address. For the second kind, MCP over HTTP is available at a fixed address, fronted by its own login server.
details.p2: When connecting, you land on an approval page stating who wants to connect and to what. Only your click grants access. This page is the actual barrier, not the protocol: without it, anyone who knows the address could at least reach the login screen.
details.p3: Granted connections then appear in your list and can be cut at any time. The HTTP access exclusively accepts access tokens, never your browser session cookie, ensuring an external website cannot speak on your behalf.

mcp-ueber-http.where: The approval page appears upon connecting.

deep-research-connector.title: A small interface for research connectors
deep-research-connector.summary: For clients that expect exactly two tools named search and fetch, there is a deliberately tiny catalog. It exists separately because those same clients struggle with one hundred and thirty tools.

details.p1: Research features of some clients expect a fixed, small surface: one tool named search, one named fetch, nothing more. If they receive the full catalog with over a hundred tools, they use it poorly or not at all.
details.p2: That is why this second, tiny catalog exists alongside it. It accesses the same search and the same pages, but only shows two doors. This allows a research feature to use your notes as a source, just as it would with a webpage.
details.p3: There is no screen for this; the client selects this catalog on its own. If you want full capabilities, connect via regular MCP access.

deep-research-connector.where: No screen: the connector selects this catalog on its own.

mcp-server.title: Agents access the same capabilities you do
mcp-server.summary: eXocortex speaks MCP, so Claude Code, Hermes, and other clients can read and write here. They get the same capabilities as the browser because both go through the same API; whatever a human can do, an agent can do too.

details.p1: MCP is the protocol through which a language model uses external tools. eXocortex includes such a server, so Claude Code, Hermes, ChatGPT, and others can search, read, write, move, comment, and build here. For you, this means your notes are accessible right where you are working anyway, instead of behind a window you have to open separately.
details.p2: All three access paths—browser, built-in AI, and external agents—go through the same API and share a single tool catalog. This is not a courtesy, but a rule in the build process: if a feature is added that a human can use, it must simultaneously be accessible to agents, or the build goes red.
details.p3: Before irreversible calls, such as permanent deletion, the server requires a second, identical request as confirmation. This is not an error, but intentional: send the same call once more, and it will be executed.

api-tokens.title: Custom access tokens with tiered permissions
api-tokens.summary: A token is explicitly given read, write, or administration permissions, instead of representing the entire account. The page also shows ready-made connection commands for common clients.

details.p1: A token is the credential a program uses to log in without knowing your password. When creating it, you specify what it is allowed to do: read-only, write as well, or administer. An empty selection permits nothing—that is the safe starting point.
details.p2: A read-only token for an evaluation can therefore break nothing, and you do not have to hand over the entire account just because a script needs a list. The token value is displayed exactly once, never again afterwards, so copy it to the right place immediately.
details.p3: Below the list are ready-to-use connection commands for common clients, with the address and token prefilled. You copy one line and you are connected, instead of hunting down a configuration file. A token can be revoked at any time.

eigene-schluessel.title: Custom provider keys per workspace
eigene-schluessel.summary: A workspace can store its own provider key instead of using the installation’s key. The key is stored encrypted and cannot be read out afterwards.

details.p1: In the settings of a workspace, you can store a dedicated key for the model provider. All AI runs for this workspace then go through that account and appear on its bill, instead of the installation’s.
details.p2: This is intended for cases where multiple people or multiple projects share an installation and each side covers its own costs. Without a custom key, the installation’s key is used silently, so nobody has to configure anything.
details.p3: The key is stored encrypted and cannot be read out afterwards, not even by administration; you can only replace or remove it. The key for decryption resides in the server configuration and not in the database.

einstellungen-geltungsbereiche.title: Settings for the installation and per workspace
einstellungen-geltungsbereiche.summary: Most toggles apply to the entire installation; many of them can be overridden in an individual workspace. An upper limit propagates downward: if you lower the value for the installation, all workspaces follow suit.

details.p1: A setting is resolved in layers: the built-in default, the environment at startup, the value for the installation, and, if present, the workspace value. No entry in the workspace means inherit, not “off”. Changes are made at runtime in administration; a restart is not required.
details.p2: Not every key can be overridden, and that is deliberate: which model responds in a workspace is its own business; how long logs are kept is not. Which keys belong to which level is fixed.
details.p3: Some values have an upper limit that propagates downward: if you lower the budget per run for the installation, all workspaces follow suit, even those that had entered a higher value before. Otherwise, a limit would not be one. Credentials are deliberately not a setting and never appear in this list.

einstellungen-geltungsbereiche.where: Administration, Settings, or a workspace’s settings.

nutzerverwaltung.title: Accounts and roles
nutzerverwaltung.summary: User administration lists all accounts, grants administration privileges to someone, disables an account, or deletes it. A disabled account immediately loses all credentials, instead of being rechecked on every request.

details.p1: The list displays all accounts with name, email, role, and status. From here, you invite someone, grant administration rights, revoke them again, deactivate an account, or delete it permanently.
details.p2: Deactivating revokes all sessions and tokens immediately, instead of checking with each request whether the account is still allowed. That is a crucial difference: a check that someone forgets to write leaves a loophole, whereas revoked access does not.
details.p3: Deleting is a further step intended for when someone should really disappear. If you only want to keep someone out, deactivating is the right choice because attribution on pages is preserved. Both can also be done via the tools.

einladungen.title: By invitation only
einladungen.summary: There is no open registration: an account is created from an invitation with an expiration date, which can be resent or revoked. This keeps the installation accessible online without being open to everyone.

details.p1: There is no registration form. An account is only created from an invitation: you enter an email address in user administration, the invited person receives a link, and uses it to set their password.
details.p2: An invitation expires, can be resent if the email landed in spam, and can be revoked if you change your mind. Pending invitations are listed so none go unnoticed.
details.p3: This is why this installation can sit openly on the web without being open to everyone. Inviting also works via the tools, meaning from within an agent.

modell-registry.title: Configure models and enable per provider
modell-registry.summary: Available models are listed with pricing and context window size per provider. A request only goes to providers that can actually serve it, rather than just the next best one.

details.p1: The same model is often offered by multiple providers, at different prices and with different context window sizes. The registry therefore maintains one row per provider and model, with price, window size, and capabilities like image understanding or tool calls.
details.p2: Before each request, a fresh decision is made about which providers can serve it at all, and only those are considered. A conversation that is too long for the small window of a cheap provider will therefore not end up there and fail halfway through. Which of the suitable providers ultimately handles it is decided by routing, unless you specify an order.
details.p3: In administration, you define which models exist at all, which one is the default, and which are used for special tasks such as summaries, embeddings, or images. You can see what a model cost in the usage overview.

anbieter-routing.title: Prefer fast providers, exclude slow ones
anbieter-routing.summary: You decide how OpenRouter chooses among the providers of a model: by throughput, latency, or price, with providers that are never picked or the only ones allowed. Each model can override individual preferences for itself.

details.p1: The same model runs across multiple providers, and their speeds vary greatly. For a long response, the generation speed is the main factor determining how long you wait: nearly ten thousand tokens take well over five minutes at 32 tokens per second, but just over one minute at 150. Without a preference, routing chooses on its own and sometimes ends up with the slowest one.
details.p2: The settings therefore contain a default for all requests, in the format that OpenRouter itself understands: sort by throughput, latency, or price, exclude providers, or only allow specific ones. Whatever OpenRouter adds in the future can be configured there as well.
details.p3: A model can change individual values without losing the rest: if it only changes the sorting, excluded providers remain excluded. Which providers can serve a request at all because their context window is large enough is still checked before each request, and sorting only applies among those.

anbieter-routing.where: Administration, Settings, AI group, and per model in Administration, AI models, when editing.

kosten.title: What AI cost
kosten.summary: Every run is logged with model, tokens, and cost, broken down by workspace and time period. This turns "what is this actually costing me" into a page rather than a guess.

details.p1: Every run is logged: which model, which provider, how many tokens in and out, what it cost, and what it belonged to. The overview aggregates this by workspace and time period.
details.p2: This answers the questions usually only answered by a provider bill at the end of the month: which workspace consumes the most, which automation is more expensive than expected, whether switching to a smaller model was worth it.
details.p3: The numbers are actual records, not estimates; they come from the provider’s per-call billing. Complete requests and responses are kept only for a configurable duration, while the numbers remain.

anmeldung.title: Sign in and reset password
anmeldung.summary: Sign-in works via email and password, a forgotten password via an emailed link. A deactivated account remains in place but can no longer do anything, preserving attribution on pages.

details.p1: You sign in with email and password. The session persists across browser restarts, so you don’t have to sign in again every morning. If you forgot your password, you send yourself a link via email from the sign-in page and set a new one.
details.p2: Deactivating an account is different from deleting it. The deactivated account remains in place, but can no longer sign in, and all its credentials are gone immediately. This keeps the author’s name on pages instead of displaying "unknown" everywhere.
details.p3: On a phone, eXocortex can be installed as an app; the address bar disappears and the share menu recognizes it.

auftraege.title: Work items: Hand over work to humans, agents, and AI
auftraege.summary: A work item records what needs to be done: objective, acceptance criteria, context pages, who is working on it, and the outcome. It persists even if an AI run fails, can wait for a person, and get a second attempt later.

details.p1: A work item can be worked on by a person, an agent account like Claude Code or Hermes, or the built-in AI. This works in all directions: you hand work to an agent, an agent hands a follow-up question back to you as a work item, or two agents pass work between each other.
details.p2: The status is an intentional decision and not a mere reflection of the last run: created, in progress, blocked, awaiting feedback, ready for review, done, failed, or cancelled. Anyone who is blocked or waiting notes down what they are waiting for.
details.p3: “Start AI run” hands the work item to the built-in AI in a separate conversation. The AI records its outcome on the work item, each run appears with its status and costs, and a budget prevents further runs from costing more than intended.
details.p4: Every change is recorded in the history, along with the name of the person or agent who made it, and for an agent also its client application. Work items can be broken down into subtasks.
details.p5: Agents work with exo_work_item_list, exo_work_item_get, exo_work_item_create, exo_work_item_update, exo_work_item_note, exo_work_item_start_run, and exo_work_item_delete.

auftraege.where: Sidebar under “Work items”, or Ctrl + K and “Open work items” or “New work item”.

aenderungsvorschlaege.title: Change proposals: agents propose, you decide
aenderungsvorschlaege.summary: Instead of editing pages directly, an agent or the built-in AI can propose changes. You see every change as a diff against the page, apply them one by one or all at once, and reject the rest with a reason.

details.p1: A proposal gathers changes to one or more pages: a block, a section, a passage of text, the entire page, or a new page. None of it appears on a page until you accept it.
details.p2: Changes are applied against the state they were proposed on. If a page has changed since then, the change is no longer written, but marked as outdated so nothing ever lands on an unreviewed state. A snapshot is created before every acceptance.
details.p3: The AI’s write mode (in Settings, or per task) sets whether it writes directly, only proposes, or only reads. For external agents, there is the token scope “Read and propose”. Both are enforced on the server, not just as a prompt request to the model.
details.p4: If a proposal belongs to a task, submitting it moves the task into review and shows it under “Waiting for you”. Once all changes are decided, the AI continues working based on your decision.
details.p5: Agents work with exo_changeset_propose, exo_changeset_submit, exo_changeset_get, and exo_changeset_list; exo_changeset_apply and exo_changeset_reject are only available for a person’s external access, never for the built-in AI.

aenderungsvorschlaege.where: Sidebar under “Proposals”, on the task, under “Waiting for you”, or Ctrl + K and “Open change proposals”.

arbeitsstaende.title: Work checkpoints: resume an interrupted task right where it left off
arbeitsstaende.summary: A work item remembers how far the work has progressed: what is done, what is still missing, what assumptions and insights exist, and which pages have been created. If an AI run aborts because a provider fails to respond, the quota is exhausted, or the run waits for an answer, the next run picks up right there, even with a different model.

details.p1: The checkpoint is mainly recorded by the AI itself, after each major step and before it stops. eXocortex adds to it automatically if the work is waiting for an inquiry or a run ends without completion: in that case, the last status is saved along with the reason for the interruption.
details.p2: “Start AI run” resumes from the latest checkpoint by default. The new run receives the checkpoint instead of the old chat history, plus all decisions made since then, and a note indicating which pages have changed in the meantime. In the same dialog, you can select a different model or start completely from scratch.
details.p3: On the work item’s page, the current checkpoint is displayed with its plan, assumptions, insights, and pages; earlier checkpoints can be expanded. Each checkpoint also appears in the history.
details.p4: A checkpoint is not a memory: it belongs to a task and is done when the task is done. Anything meant to last belongs in the agents’ memory.
details.p5: Agents work with exo_work_item_checkpoint and exo_work_item_checkpoints; exo_work_item_start_run accepts fromCheckpoint and modelSlug.

arbeitsstaende.where: On the page of a work item under “Checkpoint”, and in the “Start AI run” dialog.

wartet-auf-dich.title: Waiting for you: everything that currently needs your input
wartet-auf-dich.summary: A workspace-wide list of everything that cannot proceed without you: decisions, shares, results to review, blocked tasks, failed AI runs, and questions from agents. You reply right there, and the work picks up with your answer at the exact spot where it stopped.

details.p1: Entries are created automatically: if a task switches to “ready for review”, “blocked”, or “waiting for input”, it appears here, and once it leaves that status, it disappears again. If the last AI run of an open task fails, eXocortex asks whether you want another try or want to give up.
details.p2: Agents ask explicitly, for instance “MCP connection global or per workspace?” with the answers presented as buttons. If the built-in AI needs your decision in the middle of a task, it pauses instead of guessing: the task waits, the run finishes, and no one has to stay in the chat. When you answer, minutes or days later, it continues in the same chat with your answer and the recorded state of the work.
details.p3: Nothing appears here just because it happened. Completed entries remain traceable under “Done”, showing who chose what and when. If a task is canceled or deleted, its open entries become obsolete.
details.p4: As long as something is waiting, the header at the top right shows a hand icon with the count. Open entries for a task are also displayed at the top of its page.
details.p5: Agents work with exo_attention_list, exo_attention_get, exo_attention_request, exo_attention_resolve, and exo_attention_withdraw.
details.p6: For a share, it says precisely what is supposed to happen and which pages are affected. If one of those pages changes before you answer, your reply will no longer approve anything, and the agent asks again with the updated state. A question can also run in the background without pausing the task; the card will then let you know that work continues.

wartet-auf-dich.where: The hand icon at the top right of the header, the account menu under “Waiting for you”, or Strg + K and “Waiting for you”.
